utterances.text: Just a moment. Sir, when you are being asked questions by Mr. Vasic here, you are both speaking in the same language. It is very difficult for the interpreters to keep up with you if they have to interpret both the question and the answer and you are answering the question while they are still interpreting the question. So would you please pause after Mr. Vasic has finished speaking before you give your answer. In that way, we can all hear you far better and we can have properly recorded what it is you're saying. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you why you did not state this in the statement that you gave to the investigator of the OTP in 1996.

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it went quickly when I was questioned on that occasion. It went on quickly as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Is it for the same reason that you did not mention the occasion when a drunk colleague was kicking the door of the isolation cell and screamed at Zoran Matovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It all happened quickly and it did not occur to me -- I didn't really have time to mention this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you told us that you had heard someone mention the last name of the person which we marked as FWS-08, which is on the paper in front of you. Can you please tell us, who did you hear this last name from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know this letter. From the Serb troops that walked in the hallways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated today that your hearing problems developed after your imprisonment and after your detention in KP Dom. You also said you hear nothing on one ear and can hear poorly on your other ear. Could you please let me finish the question so that your voice does not go through, your voice is protected. So can you please tell us: How did you hear the guards mentioning this last name in the hallway and how could you communicate with the prisoner in the neighbouring cell through the wall, in view of your poor hearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, you did not understand me. I could hear well until they imprisoned me; and once I was in prison, I was beaten so badly that I couldn't hear any more after that. You simply did not understand what I told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I am -- what I am asking you pertains to this period after your beating and after you were brought to the KP Dom. How is it that you could hear this, in view of such poor hearing of yours? How could you hear the conversation of the guards in the hallway and how could you communicate with the prisoner in the neighbouring cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could hear everything well then, but this developed after I was beaten and while I stayed at KP Dom. My hearing problems started -- my ears were producing this noise, and to this date it continues. It's as if the planes -- the sound of airplanes; that's what I'm hearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, sir, you said that your left membrane bust. Could you tell us whether that was due to a blow?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it while you were beaten with rifle butts in the headquarters in Jabuka?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was beaten so badly that I could not get up for 15 days. My ears and my head, I was all bloody when I came from Jabuka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today you mentioned two individuals, Masic Elvedin and Starhonic Hasan. Can you tell us, please, if they were members of the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told by them where they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today, when asked by my learned colleague, you discussed the approximate age of these individuals. If I were to tell you that Masic Elvedin was born on 14th of September of 1972, and Starhonic Hasan on 31st of May of 1966, would you agree that that was their approximate age?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not ask them how old they were and whether they were members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask whether they were members of the JNA. I asked you whether they were members of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Masic Elvedin was wounded during his arrest and that he was treated upon coming to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you not aware of this, or you know that he was not treated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was with me but he didn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today you discussed the injuries of Ejub Durmisevic and the cut on his ear. Can you tell us whether you know -- if you know whether he was injured before he came to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- he sustained those injuries when he was arrested. He was brought there and they took a piece of cloth and wrapped it around his head, and he asked to see a doctor but nobody came to provide any medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who wrapped his ear; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I guess Serb troops; those that caught him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you mentioned that you knew that Ejub Durmisevic and Adil Karisik had disappeared. Can you tell us who did you -- who have you talked to as to whether they had been seen anywhere?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adil Karisik and Ejub Durmisevic were taken from the KP Dom at 3.00. When they came to Cajnice, I saw his wife in Gorazde, and I asked her whether she had heard anything of Ejub, and she answered, "I never heard anything."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you talked about the fear that you had when you came to KP Dom. Can you tell us whether you were afraid when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course. I was afraid immediately, and when I came to KP Dom, my life was in question. I didn't know whether I would survive, and when I was afraid, I lost the ability to speak for five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was your life in danger; when you were arrested in Jabuka?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in Jabuka and in KP Dom. And they would tell me, "You were lucky because you were caught by kind people, and had you been caught by those who kill instantly ..." then you can imagine what kind of fear it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When -- in your statement, and when asked by my learned friend colleague, you stated that soldiers beat you while they were transporting you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please wait for me to finish the question so that your voice is not carried through. So you stated that the soldiers beat you while you were transferred to KP Dom. Is this when your ribs were broken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They beat me in a car from both sides. They were beating me. And I put my hands on my heart, and they pulled my hands away, and then with their heels and rifle butts, they hit me, so around my heart, I have serious problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you please tell us whether they also beat you on your kidneys and back on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, certainly, they did, on my spine and kidneys. They kicked me from all sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also hit you with rifle butts and boots?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rifle butts and boots, heels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you state to the Security Centre that Boro Ivanovic participated in negotiations concerning your exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. While you were in Cajnice, were you interrogated by the military security?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Your Honours, Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked why you didn't mention the conditions of darkness, the freezing water, the "balija" term used by Zoran Matovic when he beat you, and why you didn't mention how you knew it was Zoran Matovic that beat you, in your previous statements, by my learned friend. Can you tell the Court about how long it took the Bosnian authorities to take your first statement? For about how many hours were you kept for questioning after you were released from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that went on for about an hour, hour and a half. It was quite fast, and I had no time to state this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the second statement, the first statement that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. gave to the Tribunal, I would like to read a portion of that statement out to you, and can you state whether, in fact, you said this? This is the 1996 statement, it's identification number 292: "I've given a previous statement which is now shown to me. I've now read it to refresh my memory. I confirm that it's my statement. I recognise the signature. My previous statement to the police was exactly what I experienced. Today I shall update my previous statement with some additional information, and I refer to my previous statement which would be incorporated into this statement." Do you remember stating that to the Tribunal investigator, that this statement would be an update of your previous one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just would like to ask you a couple of questions about Elvedin Masic and Hasan Starhonic. You were asked by my learned friend whether or not they were soldiers before being arrested at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these men from before arriving at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know how they were arrested, the circumstances in which they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, how did you know that they weren't soldiers from before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they came to my cells later on. I was there and I did not even ask them if they were -- they had been members, because I simply wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it the case that you don't know whether they were soldiers before arriving to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-159 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence before the Tribunal. You may now leave. Please wait for a moment, however, whilst the blinds are lowered so that you are able to leave the courtroom without being seen by members of the public. What is the situation about FWS-113 and protective measures, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness does not have any protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you did promise to provide us with the references in the transcript to where you have taken some issue with the question of the different amounts of food given to the Serbian prisoners and the Muslim prisoners. Are you able to give us those page references?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not turn my microphone on, Your Honours. I tried to find this part where my colleague, Mr. Vasic, asked a witness FWS-162, on page 1441 -- I apologise, 1439 and 1441. When my colleague Vasic asked the witness why, in his previous statements, he did not state that Serbs were given more food and the food was thrown away while the Muslims prisoners collected that that was thrown away. This is -- this relates to what I brought up yesterday, that this involves the extra food that Serbs were given, based on the statement of this witness. This is what I remembered most vividly; however, we did not have time to analyse all other statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're suggesting, are you, that that is a challenge to that particular witness's evidence that the Serbs had better conditions, better food, television, better accommodation, were able to go out of their room, and that they had as much food as they wanted?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday the food was discussed when you intervened on a question posed by my learned colleague, and I remember that we attempted to impeach the witness, who in his statements had never mentioned that the Serbs were given extra food that was later on thrown away, and this is exactly what my colleague Vasic asked this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you haven't asked any other witness any questions about an identical statement made by them. The fact that something is not referred to in an earlier statement may be relevant in the particular case as to whether what he says in Court is true, but you seem to give some magic to these statements that if something is not stated in the statement, then it can't be accepted as being true. The fact that that witness gave evidence which is identical to what every other witness in the case has said rather tends to suggest that he's telling the truth, despite the fact that he hadn't put it in his earlier statement. You have not challenged anybody else at all, and there are, as at the end of last year, eight witnesses who have expressly stated that the food which was given to the Muslims was considerably less than that which was given to the Serbs, and there hasn't been one question asked of them to challenge the truth of that evidence. And I'm afraid I still remain of the view that there is no real challenge to that issue at all, and it seems to me that if we're going to hear another half dozen or so witnesses telling us the same thing, we're wasting time. But if you can find something better than what your recollection is of that cross-examination, by all means come back to us, but you had better do it quickly because I propose to tell the Prosecution that is not in issue in this trial. Where is this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This witness has actually the same name as another witness we have heard at an earlier point in time. We therefore suggest that we call this witness in the proceedings Dzevad S. Lojo, "S" referring to his father's name, to be able to distinguish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I hope we'll be able to remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you please make the solemn declaration in the document which is being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. The document with the identification and pseudonyms, headed FWS-133, will be Exhibit P423 and it is under seal. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Dzevad Lojo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your birth date?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: 18th of October, 1950.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Muslim, Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. Three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Mose Pijade Street 6, in downtown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your home close to the Hotel Zelengora?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, right next to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your profession before the war?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Before the war, I was the director of the coal mine Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when did you have this job in the coal mine?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: 1st July 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you stop working there and functioning as the director?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I stopped when the aggression in Foca took place, and I couldn't go back to work after the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Before the war, I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, or rather of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you later join any of the newly-formed nationalistic parties?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No, I never joined any other party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, unrelated, actually, to your evidence and to your experiences, we heard the term "Ustasha" in evidence given by another witness. Could you explain the term "Ustasha," what it refers to?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, generally, those are the inherited means of treating the members of the military formations in this conflict. "Ustasha" is a symbol of those who were members of the formations during the Second World War. They were Croats and Muslims. And "Chetniks" was the term that was used for the members of the Serbian forces during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it was used in the '90s, was it used as an insulting term?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, in some way it was insulting. It symbolised the sides that one took in that ethnic conflict. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it mean that "Ustasha" refers to the Croats and the Muslims? It wasn't very clear from that answer. "Chetniks" is the term given to the Serbs. We know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ustasha -- you heard the question of the Presiding Judge. "Ustasha," to which ethnical groups did it relate?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992 - we are now talking about April 1992 - as you lived near the Hotel Zelengora, could you see the radio station in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, before the war, the radio station moved to the former JNA hall, which was right across from my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the radio station in Foca, was it taken over when the war started?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: On the morning of the 8th of April, people were supposed to go to work. At 8.00, or rather already at 7.00, when the driver from the mine was supposed to come and pick me up, I saw, on the windows of the JNA hall, soldiers in camouflage uniform and with weapons, on those windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they ever take over the Foca radio? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. At that moment, that morning, some paramilitary formations from the Serb side had already covered certain points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any of the broadcasts of the Radio Foca after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything related to the functioning of the Foca administration?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. This radio at first appealed during the first two or three days of the conflict for bringing the conflict to a halt while the SDA and the SDS were still negotiating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the fighting, did you hear any information on the radio how the Foca administration would function for the future?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. We did not listen to this radio very often because of all the ethnic bias that was expressed there, but there was a programme where Velibor Ostojic spoke, one of the leaders of the SDS, at republican level, that is. He said to the Serb people that from that moment onwards, Foca would flourish from an economic, political, and cultural point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you -- sorry. When did you hear this being broadcast?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, let us say that it was in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say anything in relation to the future administration in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: It went without saying that the entire territory of the municipality of Foca would be run by one people, that is, the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ostojic say that; and if so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: It is hard for me now, with all this time that has gone by, to repeat exactly what he said, but he did say what I already mentioned to you, that with the SDS at its helm, the overall administration of Foca would be set up from a political and economic point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started, where were you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I was in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in the fighting at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. No. No. I was in my apartment all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any negotiations related to a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. I did not have an opportunity to do so because I was not a member of the SDA, that is to say, of any party that would be authorised to take part in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a commission for monitoring the cease-fire considered or even established?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As I said previously, until the 8th of April, in the evening, according to what I heard over the telephone, and this was also on the radio, the leaders of the SDA and the SDS tried to reach an agreement in the municipality building for shooting to stop within and around Foca. To that end, allegedly, a cease-fire had been agreed upon which would, during those first few days, from the 8th of April onwards, be under the monitoring of joint police patrols. In order to make it possible to monitor the cease-fire and possibly to intervene, it was proposed to set up a commission consisting of three members from the Serb ethnic group and three members of the Muslim ethnic group, and I was one of the three Muslims representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who proposed you as a member?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, the Muslim side, which was represented by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you appointed to this commission although you were not an SDA member?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I assume that at that time when these proposals were being made, both sides were required to propose persons who would be respected by the other side, prominent citizens of Foca, and I believe that these were the criteria involved in the setting up of this commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was in this commission? Do you recall anyone, the name?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: (redacted), I remember that name from the Muslim side. He was deputy commander of the police at that time. And on the Serb side, Nade Radovic. I can't remember the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nade Radovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Nade Radovic. It's a man. At that time, he was the director of Temika, a factory that made household appliances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who nominated the Serbs, this person? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I assume that at this meeting where the members of the SDA and the SDS had put forth their proposals, the Serb side, the SDS proposed him, and the Muslim side proposed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Mr. Radovic, was he an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know about his party affiliation. He was a reserve captain, and allegedly, at the beginning of the war, he was a member of these Serb paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did SDS Crisis Staff operate in Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: He never publicly declared himself. It was never said that there was an official SDS Crisis Staff, but we all realised that something like that did exist and that it dealt with charting the policy that was to be pursued vis-à-vis the Muslim population; that is to say that it was involved in preparations for war and the way in which this war would be waged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? What was your information about this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, as director of the mine, I often had the opportunity of trying to forestall certain situations that could go really bad. Within my company, I had persons who were ethnic Serbs and members of the SDS and of the SPO, the Serb Renewal Movement, and I also had Muslims employed there who were members of the SDA. So I tried in this situation, in March and April, to help them find a common tongue in terms of the mine itself and the area that was covered by the mine. These were localities, Miljevina, Jelec, Kozja Luka, Kratine. That was the neighbourhood. I concentrated on that primarily after the referendum which was held on the 1st and 2nd of March, the referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because immediately after that referendum, roadblocks were set in Miljevina on the road to Sarajevo, by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we do not have to go into these political details because it's not in dispute here. My question was actually how did you hear about the Crisis Staff, the SDS Crisis Staff? Who told you about it or what other information did you have?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I got this information from Taib Lojo, who was President of the municipality, and other members of the SDA, that the Serb side, the SDS, had its Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was a member of this SDS Crisis Staff? Did you find out?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, ex officio, the president of the SDS at that time, Miro Stanic, was a member of the Crisis Staff, as well as Petko Cancar. According to the information received subsequently, when people were first taken to the camp, Zdravko Begovic was too, as well as Nade Radovic, Dr. Mandic, and others. I can't remember exactly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mandic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: He was a neuropsychiatrist, a specialist at the Foca hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he an SDS member, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a member of the SDS, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which function he has in this SDS Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever try -- did you ever contact members of this Crisis Staff, of this SDS Crisis Staff? Did you ever talk to them?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Not in that sense, as to members of the Crisis Staff, but when they first came into power, as the SDS, I contacted them often, as persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whom did you, for instance, contact?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, Miro Stanic, Petko Cancar, and others on various occasions. That is, when these authorities were established. So during the Serb holidays, Christmas and New Year, they had receptions. This was in 1991 and in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Immediately before the outbreak of the war, and even after that, did you speak to any of these persons, these SDS persons?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war started, did you try to leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: At first, no. During the first few days, we thought that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. situation would calm down and that it would not escalate into what it indeed escalated into later. As director of the mine, I was duty-bound to take care of this complex process of production so that there would not be major damage because it could all be flooded. However, when I saw that things were getting out of control, and that in that situation objectively one could not survive in Foca, I tried to get out, but it was impossible because of the situation as it then was, and also due to the position of my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was it impossible, from your apartment, to get out?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: From the very beginning, the apartment was in the area that was under the control of the Serb forces, the JNA hall, and there were snipers around the neighbouring buildings, and also on the bridges across the Cehotina and the Drina rivers. It was impossible to cross there any more, I mean to cross them safely, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 23rd of May, 1992. That is when I was taken away from home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you spend the time from the 8th of April, 1992, until your arrest?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I was in the apartment all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not go to work? I mean after the initial fighting had stopped.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As I said, after a few days, roadblocks were set and it was impossible to communicate between Foca and Miljevina. The driver didn't come either. And also, when Foca fell seven or eight days later, the SDS, or rather their leadership, appointed another person, an ethnic Serb, as director. In that period, all Muslims stopped working at all jobs. They were simply returned from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get the information that you were no longer the director but someone else?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Nobody informed me about this officially. They simply appointed their own management, without any kind of explanation or without providing any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I learned about it because telephones were still operating until the 2nd or 3rd of May in Foca, so I could make telephone calls to my own mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the new director of the mine?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Slavko Stankovic, the former director of the mine, who was director before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name us any other Muslim directors of companies that lost their position at that time?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, all positions, political and also in various firms, the mine, Focatrans, the regional medical centre, schools, the Sutjeska National Park, everywhere, in all companies. There were no exceptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they always replaced by Serbs, these former Muslim directors?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. Only ethnic Serbs. Perhaps somebody might have been a Montenegrin, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Muslim workers? Could they continue to work?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. Everybody was sent home; cleaners, medical staff, teachers, everybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: My wife is a nurse, and she could no longer go to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also hear that from your Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All of us who remained in our apartments were prevented from going to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they were prevented from going to work. Does that mean movement was restricted, officially restricted?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, there could be some movement. Usually it was women for the most part, and a man or two. It was not safe or advisable for men to move about town at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a -- was it officially also forbidden to -- for Muslims to move around at one point in time, or was --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That happened sometime around the end of April, after an event. Since there were combat contacts in one area, a group of Serb soldiers were killed, and from that moment onwards, it was broadcast over the radio, and also there was a police car with a megaphone stating that all movement in Foca was forbidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All movement of all ethnic groups or were Muslims targeted specifically?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Muslims only. There were very few Croats, so no mention was made of them, but that was understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in your home, was it ever searched?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that and what happened?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Again, this was the end of April, beginning of May. Apartments were being searched by Serb soldiers in uniform. Usually there would be three of them respectively. They would be searching apartments, looking for weapons, reportedly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say apartments were searched, all apartments or were Muslims and Croats targeted specifically?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know about the rest, but I know that, in my building, I mean at our entranceway, there is only one Serb apartment, but it's only the Muslim apartments that were searched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often was your own apartment searched?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: While I was still at that apartment, once, and afterwards, they came again -- that's what my wife told me -- but simply to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those soldiers that searched your apartment, in which capacity did they do that? Were they military policemen or just the normal soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In my case, they had no authorisation whatsoever. They simply went from one apartment to another. Two of them had white pieces of cloth on their sleeves saying that they were members of the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the fighting had ceased, did you see houses burn?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see which houses burned, if it was Muslim or Serb houses or both?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: During this first attack, this first fighting that took place from the 8th of April onwards, it is mainly Muslim houses in Prijeka Carsija, Careva that were burning. You could see the smoke from my apartment. And also in my neighbourhood, behind the JNA hall, a house burned down behind the local cinema. After the combat contacts I mentioned, until the 15th of April, in Donje Polje there were Serb houses that burned down as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned this Prijeka Carsija. What was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Prijeka Carsija is an old part of town, dating back to the Turkish times. It is resemblant of Bascarsija in Sarajevo. That is where there were small shops, small craftsmen's shops and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in your apartment, did you get any information what was going on in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, we could follow Radio Sarajevo for as long as we could hear it, and also television. Later on, we could only follow the Serb TV programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is indeed. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you mentioned that you could follow Radio Sarajevo for a while. What information did you get about what happened to Muslims in other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, at the time, it was -- we could hear on broadcast the events around Sarajevo, as well as municipalities in the southeastern part of Bosnia, Foca, Rogatica, Visegrad and Cajnice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the Muslims in these areas that you just mentioned, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: The same what was going on as Foca. In those areas, ethnic cleansing was conducted, in Visegrad, Cajnice, Rudo, in Rogatica, whereas Gorazde, as an enclave, was saved because people in that area were organised better than people in other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "ethnic cleansing," what do you mean? What does that include?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: That means that all those who are not members of Serb or Montenegrin people were expelled, locked up or eliminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "eliminated," do you mean killed actually?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested on the 23rd of May in 1992. Were you the first to be arrested in your apartment block or was -- were other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. persons arrested before that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In that building, none of the tenants were arrested, but a person who lived in my apartment was arrested because this person came from Aladza neighbourhood, because he couldn't live there any more, so he moved to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that, and when was he arrested?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: A Muslim, on May 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name of this person? But please, before you tell us the name, please check on the list -- you have a list in front of you, and if it is a person from the list, then please give us only the code number and not the name.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No, not on the list, Selimovic Erkrem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: An elderly gentleman who worked in the insurance company, from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was -- to clarify, was he arrested in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who arrested him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Same people who three days later, or rather six days later, came to pick me up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who picked you up?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Vukovic Zoran came to pick me up, and one of the Banovic brothers with a nickname Bota.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which capacity did they arrest you? Were they soldiers, military police, normal police?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: They wore military camouflage uniforms, and I don't know which position they held in the hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you on which order they arrested you, who sent them to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: At that moment, no. They simply told me to come along with them, that they were taking me to KP Dom. This is what this entity was called prior to the war. This was a prison. They also told me that I would be safer there than in my own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have an arrest warrant or any other piece of paper to present to you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, they didn't have it in my case or in the case of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only person arrested on this occasion or were others taken to the KP Dom together with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: On that occasion, I was the only one who was taken away. There was a car, a Mazda 323, that they took me in, and it was a car which belonged to the gentleman that I described to you previously, and I was the only one who was taken there on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I remained there from May 23rd until April 4th of 1993, approximately 317 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever find out why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. One couldn't find that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated when you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. I was never interrogated. From the moment I was arrested, nobody ever talked to me, nobody ever asked me anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard from other detainees and witnesses that they were interrogated. Why were you not interrogated? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know why they didn't interrogate me. However, when I came to KP Dom, other detainees told me that the interrogations were being conducted and that my turn would come as well. Because prior to that, all of them had been interrogated, and some people remained that had not been interrogated yet. However, seven days after my arrival there, those interrogations had stopped, those interrogations that had been carried out prior to my arrival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever charged or convicted while you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was indicted there and there was no proceedings instigated against anybody who was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, who received you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: The officer on duty. And there was a room at the entrance into the main building; to the left and to the right were the services of the former prison; and then there is an area where people were searched and then, after that, released into the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you searched yourself?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. One of those guards instructed me to empty my pockets, take off my shoes, my socks. He checked all of the documents that I had on me. And since I didn't have anything of value, he returned those things to me. That was my identity card, my driver's licence, and nothing else. Well, there was my cheque card pertaining to my account with Privredna Bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And were you registered? Were your particulars taken down?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As far as I know from the civilian times, there was a reception room to the left. Nobody took me there. Nobody took my personal details. I know that there was a procedure involving that. I know this from the stories told by others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those persons that dealt with you on your arrival, were they their usual prison guards or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Those were guards in uniforms from civilian times, which means that they wore blue uniforms, not military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken within the KP Dom? Into which room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: The officer on duty, the guard on duty who was in the compound, came. His name was Pljevaljcic, Vlatko. And he took me to Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Room 16. On which floor was it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were taken to Room 16 and not to any other room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that they just filled up the rooms as people came along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see that there were detainees in other rooms when you arrived? Were the other rooms full? Could you see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: When I walked in, I couldn't see how many people were in rooms. However, I could see the detainees through the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 16?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I stayed in Room 16 until the end of October, until October 31st of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many detainees were with you together in that room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: The greatest number of detainees in that room was 78.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken from Room 16 after October 1992?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I was moved to a room above it, which is Room 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I stayed there for approximately a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many detainees were with you in this room, 18?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In that room, there were some 40 to 50 people. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken next? Into which room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: After that, they took 12 of us from various rooms and they took us to Room 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this room? Was it in the same building as the other two rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Same building, same entrance, just a floor above and to the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many -- you said 12, 12 of you were taken there. What kind of detainees were taken there? Was it a selected group?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, it turned out to be a selected group - three doctors among them, two engineers, teachers, economists - people with education, except for three men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why you were singled out, this group of intellectuals, why were you singled out from the other rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know why. I can only suppose that the reason for that was perhaps communication with other people who remained in these other two rooms, 16 and 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "communication"? Did they want to avoid communications with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, they tried to prevent both external and internal communication in all possible ways. They wanted us to be as isolated as possible. They didn't want us to encourage each other because there were people that had some psychological difficulties that went through some difficult times and we would encourage them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually encourage people, and if so, how? How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could, I tried to spread optimism around, to tell people that everything would take a good turn because, at that time, we supposed that most of us that were taken away were released. We didn't know what really happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Room 21?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I stayed there until April 4th, which is when I was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those people you met in the various rooms, what ethnicity did they have?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: They were all Muslims, almost, maybe two or three gypsies, some Albanians, and two or three Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the variety of age of these detainees, what was it? Well, who was the youngest and who the oldest?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Fifteen to 80 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you all civilians or was there any soldier, Bosnian soldier, among you? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Those who were apprehended, that were brought in in April, May, June, were mostly civilians who were brought in from their homes, from the streets, from hospital, from their offices. Later on, they were bringing in wounded, allegedly from Gorazde and other areas where they had been imprisoned. However, they were in isolation cells and there were very few of them, perhaps only a couple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were sick people -- detainees among you, in the rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In Room 12, where we were transferred, we found there four elderly men who had been brought in in August from Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said Room 12. Is this the --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I apologise. The room was 21. There were 12 of us. There were 12 of us brought in there. And when we came, we found four men there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- please have a look at the list and do you know any particular person who was sick that you met in the rooms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Not on this list, but on my list, there was Fehim Cengic, (redacted) (redacted)-- no, no. Can I consult my document?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness, as one of the previous witnesses this week, has also compiled documents that are actually in the trial binders, and they are the document 215 and 215A, which would be the translation, and I assume that the witness has this document in front of him and would like to consult them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have little doubt that Mr. Bakrac will ask to see the original to compare it with the copy, and he may have a justification for doing so because the last time the copy didn't quite accord with the original.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So if you would show Mr. Bakrac the original so he can compare it with document 215.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I think that you have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have copies. Let's first -- if you find out the document -- I have here a document in handwriting, not printed but handwriting. Do you have this document with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. I turned over the original, and what I have is a document that was -- that is handwritten and written in printed letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean it's something different from document 215?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, it's actually -- document 215 consists of two different sets of documents. One is in handwriting, printed -- in printed letters but still handwriting, and the other one is also handwriting but with a different pen and with -- in handwriting as a person writes. Maybe it's easier for the witness to check when we've put a set of documents -- show him first what we have in the trial binders and let him look at what he has. 215, the handwriting set of documents, starting actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it wouldn't be a bad idea to see if the witness could perhaps remember before he's allowed to look into the document. Perhaps the witness can reproduce, based on his memory, who was where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that, if I may say so, overlooks the whole of this procedure. If you want him to undergo a memory test, what does that prove? That he can remember things well. If we accept his evidence -- you can challenge it if you like, but if we accept his evidence that he made these notes at an early stage, why shouldn't we have the benefit of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour. I simply want to see if the witness could initially perhaps remember this on his own, and, if not, then he could probably look into his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, unless you can persuade us that this is some form of memory test to see how long people can remember things, I don't see any value in that, frankly, but you will have to get the provenance of the notes, if I may so describe it; when he made them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And let's see when he made them to see whether they have a better value than a memory test today.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please have a look at the handwritten with the dark pen, and please look at it and then tell -- when did you make these notes?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I made those notes in April, in Zagreb, or rather, Samobor. It was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you make these notes?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: When I left the camp and went back to my family, when my wife asked me where her two brothers were -- when I asked her, she said that she had not heard from them, and they left supposedly for an exchange in August and September of 1992. And this prompted me to verify what had happened with the others, and I concluded that most of the people that went supposedly for an exchange are missing. Then I attempted to compile a list and to distribute it to all of those who could perhaps check what happened to these people, because I was absent from the front line and Bosnia was isolated in the communication sense. And then I wrote this down about the events, about people, and through Split I forwarded it to Sarajevo so that it can be of assistance, so that it could be used as a supplement to the statements of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you wrote these notes, was it from your own memory or did you ask other people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: This was compiled based on my own memory, because when we were leaving the camp, we were not allowed to take anything with us. They were taking everything away from us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you forwarded it to others. To whom did you actually forward your notes?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Above -- on the top of this sheet there is a name. I don't know this person, but it is stated here "for Isanovic, Zaim."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know this person. This was simply an intermediary who was in the position to forward this information to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says here on the document - actually, on the top of it, "for Amira Imamovic." Who would that be?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: It's stated "Amira Isanovic," and then she in turn was supposed to forward it to Emir Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And what did you actually want to happen with your notes that you sent to this person in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I wanted this to serve as a document that could assist the relevant bodies that were researching what happened to the missing persons that were researching the camps, and I also wanted to determine what was the fate of these people that were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have also a document here with printed --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this be shown to the witness as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, the one you've been dealing with is the one headed "Information"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the one you described as having a heavy pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's joined-up handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the next one is headed, as I understand it, names with dates, and that's the one in printed handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you would please look at this document in printed writing. When did you write this? Is it -- first of all, is it your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's mine, but it's just that I tried to take care of these previous documents in this way. In the meantime, I learned some more names, so this piece of information contains some more names than the previous one did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you write this particular document?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Also in 1993, immediately after the talks I had in May, at the Red Cross in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you learned some more names. How did you learn these more names? Was it again from your memory or were these names mentioned to you by other people?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: There were two other men in Zagreb with me who had been in the camp with me before that, but also I got a lot of information from the International Red Cross. This lady there had in her computer a survey of all persons who had been registered before that, either through the Serb authorities, as far as Foca was concerned, at least, or also in terms of Red Cross visits. However, in Foca there hadn't been any such thing before that. But then in the computer there were some names, and I had not realised that before, and it says: By these names, such-and-such a person is in camp, according to the register of the Serb authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you wrote these particular notes related to these additional persons, did you remember these persons and did you remember when they were taken away, or did you get this information otherwise?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. No. I knew. In the previous information, I wrote one name, two names, five names, whatever, but I wrote the number of these persons. I could not have known all the names and surnames of the persons from other rooms who had not had direct contact with me. Usually there would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. be names. For example, one, two persons from my room. Because when people were being taken away, their names were usually called out from different rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the copies or an example of these two documents that were just shown to you within your notes, that you have today with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you mean, "examples"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two documents, these two documents that you have just looked onto, do you have either the original or your personal copy within your notes that you today brought to the Court?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No. No. I have the same copies that you have because I handed in the originals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but the Defence counsel would like to check the documents that you brought in today to see if it is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. I think that what he would like to see is the original document to compare it with what is now being used as a copy, and that's a justifiable request.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He says that he handed them in to the Prosecution, or at least to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, but this is what we actually have in the trial binders. I mean, we have to go back to the Evidence Unit if we really want to see the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't have the originals now on me, and I would have to find someone to go to the Evidence Unit and get the originals. I don't know how long this will last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You know, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, this has been raised before other Trial Chambers, but we are entitled to the original documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the Prosecution's claim to have some sort of ownership in the exhibits is not right. I'm not suggesting that's why you've done it, but there has to be a recognition that originals should be produced in Court wherever possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually thought the witness would have the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that, but he says he's given them to the Prosecution or to its investigators, so I think they should be provided. That doesn't mean we can't proceed with the right of Mr. Bakrac to check them against the originals later. First of all, we've got to hear what Mr. Bakrac wants to say about the use of these documents at all. But at some stage he must be entitled to check them against the original, if only because we have, unfortunately, had some copies which are not true copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we will provide it tomorrow. I hope we can -- I think we will be able to get it as soon as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, Mr. Bakrac, here we have two documents. I think they can be dealt with separately. The first one was of the witness's own composition and he wrote them in April 1993. Now, why should we not allow him to rely upon those notes rather than put him through some memory test of dates and names?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness explained just now the way in which this was done, and the Defence is not opposed to this at all. We thought that it would perhaps be more expedient and more useful for the Defence if we were to check this witness's credibility to see whether he recalls the facts that he is talking about. We understand this problem with the photocopies as well. We know that sometimes originals are not accessible. We know that there are photocopies, and the Defence will probably have situations in which it will not be able to provide originals but photocopies only. So we do not insist on this. We do not insist on matching this with the original before the witness says what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. But in relation to your suggestion that you wanted to test his credibility, this is something which we run into all the time in these cases. Sometimes, as I said earlier, it is an issue of credibility as to whether or not something had been put in a statement given to a Prosecution investigator back when first investigated but then gives evidence in Court here. That is relevant to credit. But to suggest that it goes to a witness's credit that he can't remember details such as this which he recorded back in 1993 today seems to me to be a completely wrong approach to how you could cross-examine a witness. It could be no suggestion that he is not telling the truth if he is unable to reproduce that detail now. It may say something for his memory, but that doesn't mean that he's not telling the truth. Now, we are interested in the truth, and surely the truth is more likely to have been recorded back in 1993 than reproduced by memory now. So unless you can produce some better argument, in my view, we should proceed by allowing the witness to refer to his document, documents made in 1993. You, of course, must get access to the original when it is produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, that is the ruling of the Trial Chamber. So you proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, by allowing the witness to give evidence from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have followed and you are allowed to consult your notes. And I had asked you whether there were any sick people among you in the three rooms that you were in. Can you give us the names of some of these sick people and tell us what they actually suffered from?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I can. In Room 16, there was a serious heart patient, 80 years old, Hasan Hadzimuratovic. He was brought from the hospital sometime in the month of May. There was an old man, Fehim, from Miljevina, also in Room 16, 78 years old. He used a crutch. Also in the upper room was Sandal, who died after my time in the KP Dom, an elderly man, sick. And I have already mentioned four elderly men and a patient in Room 21. That is the Cengices and Mirvic. But in Room 16, there were also some younger men, some men who had been wounded, or rather injured, not wounded in combat. Two or three men were brought in from hospital who had previously been brought in from Visegrad. They had been wounded by bullets or explosives. But three young men from Gorazde had had an accident on the 3rd or 4th of April, that is to say, before any kind of fighting broke out. As such, they had been put into the Foca hospital. Afterwards, when the Serb forces entered the hospital, they cleansed it of all who were not Serbs, so they brought the three of them to the KP Dom as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those sick people that you just mentioned, did they get proper treatment, medical treatment, while they were in the rooms with you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, it certainly was not adequate treatment, proper treatment, but at first a physician came to the KP Dom, or rather the camp, and then people who complained of pain went to see him and would then be given certain medicines. However, you must realise that you cannot get the same kind of treatment in a room with 80 other persons as you can under different circumstances, especially not for the elderly, for heart and asthma patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that a doctor came to the KP Dom. In which -- how often did he come? Was he there all the time or what?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: From time to time, not always. In the morning -- well, how many times a week? That, I don't know. Was not every day but I don't know how many times a week. At first, as I said, he came more often. Later on, it all boiled down to one male nurse who was a retiree who was previously employed by the KP Dom, and he had some drugs in this makeshift pharmacy of the KP Dom, and he would give whatever drugs he had to those persons who asked for them. I mean, he was fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that later it boiled down to this nurse. What is "later"? Can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, let's say sometime from August until I was there altogether, it was his interventions only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned this particular group in Room 21. Was there a Safet Avdic among you? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you -- when did you meet him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, wait a moment. That answer "yes" could have been either to, "Do you know him," or, "Was he in the room with you". I think you should make that very clear because this is a point that has been raised. It is of some importance, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when did you meet Mr. Safet Avdic in the KP Dom for the first time? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I met him as soon as I arrived on the 23rd of May. I mean I saw him. It's not that I met him. I saw him, because he had been brought in before that, on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you share, if ever -- did you ever share a room with Mr. Avdic while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: From the 31st of October until I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which room was that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was before that, before the end of October; in which room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, that room was above number 18. I don't know the exact Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. number. Was it Room 22, as it was known? He was in a group where persons from Montenegro were, or rather, persons from Jelec via Kalinovik and Bileca or from other parts of Montenegro, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Did he later tell you or did you actually see him --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No, he would pass by our room. He used the same entrance, the same entrance to the building. I mean, he went out through the same door that we went out through from Room 16. And let me explain how come we know each other so well. We are first cousins. My mother and his mother are sisters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, besides the rooms, were there -- you have already mentioned -- how many detainees were in the isolation cell? Could you ever count them or do you have any other information as to their number?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As for the isolation cells, they were by the same door but to the left-hand side from our rooms. We would find out from time to time whether two or three or four men were there on the basis of the meals that were carried in the direction of these isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of persons were kept in the isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: A number of men were kept there before they were taken to other rooms. That is to say, they were brought in and sent directly to the isolation cells. Usually, these were people who were brought in during the night. Also, there were men who were mistreated in various ways. When I say "mistreated," I am saying that they were beaten as they were brought in. And also, from time to time, people from various rooms were sent to isolation cells according to the criteria of the security people, if they had violated a rule, whatever they thought. Perhaps they had taken more food or done something else that did not fit into the regular regimen, and that is why they were taken to isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the sound of beating or screaming from these isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
