utterances.text: From the isolation cells? No. They were quite far away. I mean, there were several walls between us as an obstacle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see a person coming to your room, whatever room it was, coming from the isolation cell with injuries?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In three cases. Zaim Cedic being the first, with a degree in law, he worked in the Sutjeska National Park. Halim Dedovic, who was brought in from his home and then he spent two or three nights in the isolation cell and then he was brought to our room. And then you see what a man who was black and blue looks like. And Sacir Smajkan, with a degree in law, and he was a magistrate, a judge, in the municipal court. After having spent about 30 days in the isolation cell, he was brought into our room with visible bruises and wounds still. All three of these men are missing until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we have to go from one to the other. First, let's speak about Zaim Cedic. That's actually Schedule B, number 11. When did he come into your room and into which room, actually?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I have to digress a bit. A few days before I was brought into the camp, during the night, in front of the Zelengora Hotel, we heard a man screaming and moaning. Obviously he was being tortured badly. Afterwards, it turned out that it was that man, Zaim Cedic, who came to my room, Room 16, and told us that on that occasion, the local Serbs brought him in, the members of the Serb army, and that that night they tortured him in front of the hotel, beat him and made him swallow a significant quantity of salt. I don't know whether it was half a kilo or more. When he was brought to our room from the isolation cell, he still had visible signs all over his body, on his head, on his back, everywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long had he stayed in the isolation cell? Did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I said a few days before I was there, and then -- well, it's hard to remember but let's say it's about 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you if he was also beaten in the isolation cell or in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that these persons who were in isolation cells and who were then brought to our room never said that anyone had beat them in the isolation cells or that anything like that was done to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that he disappeared from the KP Dom. How did he disappear from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. He was taken away in a group. Now, I'd have to look at those dates again but then you have these copies of that list in front of you. It's either the 19th of August --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please check your own notes, but according to what I see in this handwriting, it's on the 19th of August, 1992. You mentioned a group and there are --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, the 19th, the 19th. I said so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you have written down here the group --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have written down into your notes a group of people. You have written down -- if you look yourself, you have written down in your notes, 20 men were taken out on that day, and you have listed several names as well.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. These are the names of the persons from my room, Room 16, whereas the others are from other rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Cedic or any other of these from your room ever heard of afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned as the second person, Halim Dedovic. And that is Schedule B, number 13. Who was he and when did he come to your room?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: The local barber, well-known in Foca. He was brought in in June, the beginning of June. As I said, he was not in the isolation cell for more than one or two nights. He was brought in in the evening, and after one or two nights he was brought to our room, Room 16, with visible injuries on his head and body, so he was black and blue. We tried to help him to the best of our ability. We used onions and salt, different compresses, so that he could walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: What I know is what he said to us. That is, that he was beaten from his home to the KP Dom, as they were bringing him to the KP Dom, and that's about two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What became out of him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: He was taken away in a group in the month of December, the 11th of December. A journalist was there too who was brought from an isolation cell, a Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have listed these incident -- you have listed -- in your document, you have listed 11th December, 1992, eight men, and you mention Mr. Dedovic, and this Slovene journalist --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues]... were they from your room, all those you have listed here?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No, they were not from my room. They were brought that night and were brought to a room above us. From my room, from 18, from 16, and this journalist, Krivograd. Later on, I found out he was directly taken from the isolation cell on that morning. That was the 11th. It was around 7.00 in the morning. They were taken to the gate and later on, they have never been heard from since. His paper Mladina established contact with me while I was in Zagreb in 1993. They tried to find out what had happened to that journalist of theirs but they never did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Sacir Smajkan. Who was he and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I stated that he was a lawyer. He was a judge in the municipal court. Prior to that, he was a misdemeanour magistrate. He was a good, solid young lawyer, judge. He was taken from his home. Based on what he said, they had intention of killing him, and he was taken to Velecevo across the Cehotina River and there he was beaten, and prior to that, they mistreated him and they -- as a result of that, he fell into the river. He managed to hide under the ivy tree. They went looking for him to finish him off. He managed to hide so that they did not find him. In the morning, he crossed the Cehotina river and went to Cohodar Mahala settlement. There he was observed by a girl, and he tried to establish contact with his friend, a Serb, who worked in MUP. However, police was quicker than him and they, in the end, took him to KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you see him in the KP Dom? When was that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, again, that was sometime in the beginning of July, because he spent quite a long time in the isolation cell. I believe a month to month and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw him, what did he look like? Did he have injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. He had difficulty walking. He had a very serious injury that could not be treated while he was in the camp. His neck vertebra was injured and there was a very deep cut there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you where he received this cut and who did it?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, once again, those were members of the local Serb forces, and that took place when he was -- after he was picked up from his house and as they were taking him to be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What became of him? Did he also disappear from the KP Dom or is he still --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. He disappeared on the 22nd of August. Yes, 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: And once again, from my room. And the wounded persons from Gorazde were in the same group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people was that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned that there were about 20 or perhaps 17 men in that group. I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were in the KP Dom, what was the highest numbers of detainees at any time? What do you estimate?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't keep track of the exact number, because the numbers were changed from time to time as people were taken away, but at one time there were between five and six hundred people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you estimate? How many detainees passed through the KP Dom altogether?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, during investigation I already stated that it was about 1.000, and that includes the people who were brought in in April and May, before me, among which there were women and children, and there was also a large group of workers from Miljevina who were brought in and then released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left in March 1993, how many detainees remained behind?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. April 1993. How many remained behind?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Eighty-one, of those that could be counted in three rooms, not including the isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have heard from other detainees that there were also Serb prisoners in the KP Dom. Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: There were. They were mostly Serb soldiers in uniform, and they were there due to various reasons. Based on what we heard, one of them had killed three of his colleagues. They stayed in the room below Room 21. Occasionally -- and from time to time there would be between 10 and 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have already discussed with other witnesses the details of the conditions in the KP Dom, and they were also compared with the conditions of the Serbs, so we do not need to go into details. I have just a very few particular questions to ask. In relation to the conditions in winter, we know from other witnesses that there was no heating in the building. Did the Serb prisoners have anything to keep warm?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Not only they had things to keep them warm, but they also had freedom of movement, and due to the fact that there was no power and all the cooking devices were powered electrically and the kettles used for cooking the food were outside, the fire was used to cook food, and we could see them walking about, and the door of the room in which they were kept was open. So one couldn't compare their conditions with ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's understood. But the question is: Did they have a stove? Could they -- did they have heating devices in this winter that you were detained?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. They and the guards, they had a stove, and they had no trouble bringing in coal or firewood into their rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see that, that they brought in firewood and coal?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. They would pass our rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the hygienic conditions of the Serb detainees better than those of the Muslims; and if so, what was different?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, we took care of the sanitary and hygienic conditions ourselves, so we did our own laundry, our own cleaning. We organised it ourselves as far as we could. Now, to what degree Serbs were able to do that, I don't know; however, they were allowed visits by members of their families, so they would be in a position to get fresh, clean clothes. And they also had other benefits available to them if they needed it, and they had an access to the bathroom and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a laundry in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you get towels or whatsoever from the laundry, and could the Serbs do that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: In the beginning, for some 45 days, when I came in, initially we were able to take a bath. In the beginning, none of us were given bed linen or anything else like that, other than soap from time to time. Afterwards, after a few months, perhaps, during the time I was there, the bed linen would be changed normally once or twice a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the Serb prisoners? Did they have better access to the laundry, the linens and towels, than the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Definitely. They could have as many as they needed. I remember a time in winter months, as groups were leaving, we tried to get three or four blankets instead of just two, just to keep warm. You have to know that in January of 1993, the temperature was at one point minus 23. There was one centimetre of ice on the walls in my room, so if you had a bottle of water, it would freeze overnight in my room. And in one moment, I don't know why, but the guards came in and ordered us to return all the blankets in excess of the two that we were allotted, and they pressured us, they threatened us. On that occasion, Safet Avdic -- people were just trying to get by and sewing blankets from pieces that they had, so Safet Avdic was taken to the isolation cell because of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have learned from other witnesses already that the food was actually starvation rations. Was no food available because of the war or were the conditions deliberately kept so bad? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: That was done on purpose, judged on all human laws. Nobody can convince me otherwise. Because in the beginning of the war, Foca was quite well supplied with food. Serb forces took over the mill in Ustikolina, which had a capacity of over 40.000 tonnes of wheat, and let's say that only half of that remained. I know that they used trucks to transport wheat, because I saw from my window convoys driving away that wheat. Also, in Kosora, which is a part of Ustikolina, there were military warehouses in which, in addition to ammunition and weapons, there were good materiel reserves. And Perucica, a trading company, before the war was one of the strongest companies in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which had federal food reserves under its supervision. What did they do with the food, I really don't know. I know that the food was not to be found in the stores either, because they simply stole it. From my apartment, in April, I could see that two stores that were there were robbed within four or five days, robbed by paramilitary forces. When I say "paramilitary," I mean the White Eagles and the forces that were present there from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see that food was delivered into the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. Below my room there was a warehouse, a makeshift one, in which they stored the food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of food was delivered? Were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Those were cans, mostly cans of 10 to 20 kilos, with canned vegetables in them, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get this food?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally suffer any physical consequences due to the living conditions in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Physically, yes. I lost weight. If that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anything else than the weight loss?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As far as physical harassment is concerned, nobody touched me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer any physical results in relation to the sanitary conditions?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: As far as the sanitary conditions are concerned, one person from our room, Alic Uzeir, and another person from another room, worked at the poultry farm in Velecevo, and he brought in lice, which he then gave to all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the living conditions affect you mentally?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I tried as much as I could to maintain my mental good health; however, consequences are unavoidable because one cannot live through -- go through life without remembering those events. Perhaps the life as it is now does not allow me to go back to those times very frequently, but one still does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever complain about the living conditions to the authorities in the camp or to the guards?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I think that complaining would not be received well under those circumstances. There were individuals who wrote complaints to the management of the camp. Among them was Alija, a salesman from Gorazde. He complained about living conditions. And based on the guards' recommendation, he wrote a letter to the KP Dom warden, asking to see him. He wrote this letter. That was late August/early September of 1992. That letter was supposedly handed in, and one or two days later he was called out and he never returned, and he is still missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were not mistreated in the KP Dom personally, you did not suffer any physical consequences. Were you ever beaten or slapped while you were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, there was one event, not directed against me. However, on the 30th of October of 1992, my room at that moment was having lunch, and as we were finishing our lunch, those who finished first would go towards the stairs that were leading from the dining room. We waited there for everyone to join us, to form a column, and to be escorted by a guard back to the room. And as we were gathering there, three men came into the compound, escorted by Krsto, a cook. I cannot remember his last name. They had automatic weapons on them, knives. One of them had a machine-gun. When they saw our group, they started towards us, shouting "balijas" at us and shouting, "Here are chickens to be slaughtered." They asked us to put our hands behind our backs, to put our heads down, and they were circling us with those weapons. Several of us, based on their assessment, did not put our heads low enough, and those of us were hit with rifle butts. So they hit me as well passing by me; however, I did not consider this to be significant. Other detainees who could see this from their rooms were in great fear. The guards started panicking, and they moved to prevent some -- to prevent this incident from escalating. They took us back to our rooms swiftly, they locked us up and did not let anybody out until these three soldiers left the compound, these three armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides you, who else was hit with rifle butts? Do you recall who was in this group? If you would please use the number.

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I -- this name is not written correctly; however, the initials are correct: FWS-214. This is a doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall anyone else who was hit on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: I don't know. There were several of men. We were so afraid because the weapons were pointed at us that one simply could not remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the incident in the indictment 5.12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that these were three men. Do you mean soldiers? Did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did soldiers have free access to the prison compound?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Based on what I know and what I could observe, there was supposedly a rule that nobody who was armed was allowed into the compound. However, individuals or groups in military uniforms would come into our compound in larger or smaller groups, especially when they were mining the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there was a rule. Do you mean the rule from pre-war or do you mean a rule now newly established? What rule do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Well, this was just my assessment. I don't know that there is a document or an official regulation regarding this. And people with personal weapons were admitted in, perhaps with a pistol, but not with a weapon, not with a rifle. And I also have to remind you that there were machine-guns in the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want a clarification. When you say, "supposedly there was a rule that armed soldiers could not get in," what kind of rule do you refer to? Who set that rule and how do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's already said he doesn't --

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: No, I don't know about this rule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other prisoners being beaten; see, really personally see with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see them being beaten, but I did see them come in beaten up, which means that they were taken away and then brought in with injuries. We could also hear when they were beaten. We couldn't see this physically because the glass was coloured over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I come to -- we will come to this section, but do you -- did you ever see a person, really see a person being beaten?

utterances.speaker: DZEVAD S. LOJO
utterances.text: Yes. There was one event which took place in June or July - I can't tell you exactly - and the food was poor and people were hungry, and that affected them and they wanted to get more food than they were given. And as we went to lunch, we would line up in order as we approached the line, and the guard who escorted us into the dining room would normally stand in the middle of the dining room. And some individuals tried to come -- to go back to the line to get a second serving without being observed by the guard. And on one occasion a guard named Vukovic noticed that the people were trying to get into the line for the second time, and he used a disproportionate force and beat up an elderly man, Selimovic, in front of us. We were sitting in a group and dining.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would now come actually to the complex of these beatings more heard than seen. I don't think I should start with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You always seem to get those extra few minutes off.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I can continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, that's all right. We will resume again tomorrow at 9.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
